screens.title: Configuring Diagnostic Settings for Azure App Services
screens.narratorSegment: When working with Azure App Services, configuring the right diagnostic settings is your first step towards comprehensive monitoring. Beyond the basic HTTP and console logs, you'll want to enable specific settings to capture detailed application-level data. For instance, 'Application logging' allows you to capture logs generated directly by your code, such as Console. Write Line in. NET or console. log in Node. js. You have the option to route these to the 'Filesystem' for quick debugging in development, or, preferably for production, to 'Blob storage' or a 'Log Analytics workspace' for scalability and centralized analysis. 'Web server logging' provides invaluable insights into incoming HTTP requests, including status codes and latency, which helps you understand traffic patterns and identify potential bottlenecks. Furthermore, 'Detailed error messages' can capture full stack traces for HTTP 500 errors, giving you precise information for debugging critical failures. Lastly, 'Failed request tracing' is a powerful tool for diagnosing specific slow or failing requests, providing an XML-based trace of the entire request pipeline. Each of these settings plays a vital role in providing a complete picture of your App Service's health and performance, allowing you to quickly pinpoint and resolve issues.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Configuring Diagnostic Settings for Azure App Services

Key Diagnostic Settings for App Services

Application Logging

Captures logs generated by your application code (e.g., Console.WriteLine). Essential for debugging application logic.

  • Filesystem: Quick for dev/test, limited retention.
  • Blob Storage: Scalable, cost-effective for long-term storage.
  • Log Analytics: Preferred for centralized analysis and querying in production.

Web Server Logging

Records details about incoming HTTP requests to your web application. Provides insights into traffic and user behavior.

  • HTTP Logs: Request method, URL, status code, latency, client IP.
  • Traffic Analysis: Understand popular endpoints and potential load issues.
  • Security Auditing: Track access patterns and suspicious requests.

Detailed Error Messages

Captures full stack traces for HTTP 500 errors. Invaluable for diagnosing server-side exceptions.

  • Developer Debugging: Provides exact code locations of failures.
  • Production Readiness: Helps quickly resolve critical application crashes.
  • Security Note: Be cautious exposing these directly to end-users.

Failed Request Tracing

Provides an XML-based trace of the request pipeline for slow or failing requests. Deep dive into request processing.

  • Performance Bottlenecks: Pinpoint where latency is introduced.
  • Request Flow: Understand how IIS/Kestrel processes a request.
  • Complex Diagnostics: Ideal for intricate request-response issues.
Key Takeaway

A combination of application, web server, error, and tracing logs provides a comprehensive view of App Service health, crucial for effective debugging and performance management.

screens.title: Configuring Diagnostic Settings for Azure Functions
screens.narratorSegment: Just like App Services, Azure Functions require careful configuration of diagnostic settings to ensure you capture all relevant telemetry. For serverless workloads, your primary focus will be on 'Function App Logs' and 'Streaming Logs'. Function App Logs are comprehensive, encompassing host logs, controller logs, and logs specific to your individual functions. These logs are vital for understanding the runtime behavior of your functions, including startup events, execution details, and any errors that occur within your code. Streaming Logs, on the other hand, provide real-time output from your functions, which is incredibly useful for immediate debugging during development or when troubleshooting live issues. For production environments, it's highly recommended to route both Function App Logs and Streaming Logs to a Log Analytics workspace. This centralizes your log data, making it easily queryable with KQL and enabling advanced analysis. Furthermore, enabling 'Application Insights' for Azure Functions is a game-changer. Application Insights provides a much richer set of telemetry specifically tailored for serverless execution, including insights into cold starts, execution duration, and crucial dependency calls. This deep visibility helps you optimize performance and identify external service bottlenecks, which are common in distributed serverless architectures. By combining these settings, you gain a complete picture of your function's health and performance.

Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Configuring Diagnostic Settings for Azure Functions

Essential Diagnostic Settings for Azure Functions

Function App Logs

Comprehensive logs covering host, controller, and function-specific events. Critical for understanding runtime behavior.

  • Host Logs: Information about the Function App runtime itself.
  • Controller Logs: Details on how requests are routed to functions.
  • Function-Specific Logs: Output from your individual function code.

Streaming Logs

Provides real-time log output from your functions. Ideal for immediate debugging and live troubleshooting.

  • Real-time Feedback: See logs as they are generated.
  • Quick Diagnostics: Rapidly identify issues during development or live incidents.
  • Temporary View: Best for short-term, interactive monitoring.

Application Insights Integration

Highly recommended for Azure Functions, providing rich telemetry specific to serverless execution and dependency calls.

  • Cold Starts: Monitor and optimize function startup times.
  • Execution Duration: Track performance of individual function runs.
  • Dependency Calls: Gain visibility into external service interactions.
  • Distributed Tracing: Trace requests across multiple functions and services.
Key Takeaway

For Azure Functions, routing Function App Logs and Streaming Logs to Log Analytics, combined with Application Insights, provides a robust and detailed monitoring solution for serverless workloads.

screens.title: Automating Diagnostic Settings with Azure CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Manually configuring diagnostic settings through the Azure portal can be tedious and error-prone, especially across multiple resources. This is where the Azure Command Line Interface, or CLI, becomes incredibly valuable. The Azure CLI allows you to programmatically define and apply diagnostic settings, ensuring consistency and enabling automation as part of your infrastructure-as-code practices. Let's walk through an example of how to configure diagnostic settings for an Azure Function App to route its logs and metrics to a Log Analytics workspace. First, we define variables for our Function App name, its resource group, and then we retrieve the ID of our Log Analytics workspace. This workspace ID is crucial because it tells Azure Monitor where to send the collected data. The core command is az monitor diagnostic-settings create. We specify a name for our diagnostic setting, the resource group, the target resource which is our Function App, and importantly, its resource type, which is Microsoft. Web slash sites even for Function Apps. Finally, we define the logs and metrics categories we want to enable, such as Function App Logs and All Metrics, and specify our Log Analytics workspace ID. This approach ensures that your monitoring configuration is repeatable, scalable, and integrated into your deployment pipelines, reducing manual effort and potential misconfigurations.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Automating Diagnostic Settings with Azure CLI

Azure CLI for Function App Diagnostics

# Assuming you have an existing Function App and Log Analytics Workspace
# Replace placeholders with your actual resource names

FUNCTION_APP_NAME="my-cohortia-functionapp"
FUNCTION_APP_RG="MonitorDemoRG"
WORKSPACE_ID=$(az monitor log-analytics workspace show \
    --resource-group "MonitorDemoRG" \
    --workspace-name "CohortiaLogWorkspace" \
    --query id -o tsv)

az monitor diagnostic-settings create \
    --name "FunctionAppToLogAnalytics" \
    --resource-group $FUNCTION_APP_RG \
    --resource $FUNCTION_APP_NAME \
    --resource-type Microsoft.Web/sites \
    --workspace $WORKSPACE_ID \
    --logs '[{"category": "FunctionAppLogs", "enabled": true, "retentionPolicy": {"enabled": false, "days": 0}}]' \
    --metrics '[{"category": "AllMetrics", "enabled": true, "retentionPolicy": {"enabled": false, "days": 0}}]'

Command Breakdown

Resource Identification

Define your Function App's name, resource group, and retrieve the Log Analytics Workspace ID for routing.

az monitor diagnostic-settings create

The core command to create a new diagnostic setting. Specify a unique name for the setting.

Target Resource & Type

Point to your Function App using --resource and its resource type (Microsoft.Web/sites).

Log & Metric Categories

Specify which log categories (e.g., FunctionAppLogs) and metrics (AllMetrics) to enable and route to the --workspace.

Key Takeaway

Using Azure CLI for diagnostic settings ensures consistent, automated, and scalable monitoring configurations for your Azure Function Apps.

screens.title: Unlocking Insights with Kusto Query Language (KQL)
screens.narratorSegment: Once your logs and metrics are flowing into Log Analytics, the real power of Azure Monitor comes alive through the Kusto Query Language, or KQL. KQL is a sophisticated, read-only query language designed for exploring and analyzing large volumes of data efficiently. Think of it as the S Q L for your operational data, but with a more intuitive and powerful syntax for time-series analysis and pattern detection. Mastering KQL is a critical skill for any Azure developer, as it allows you to transform raw log entries into meaningful insights. You can use KQL to filter out noise, aggregate data to see trends, project specific columns to focus on relevant information, and even join data from different tables to correlate events across your application and infrastructure. For example, you might query for all errors in a specific time window, summarize request counts by endpoint, or identify performance anomalies. Without KQL, you'd be sifting through mountains of text, but with it, you can quickly pinpoint issues, understand root causes, and make data-driven decisions to improve your application's reliability and performance. It's the key to truly understanding what's happening within your cloud environment.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Unlocking Insights with Kusto Query Language (KQL)

What is Kusto Query Language (KQL)?

KQL is a powerful, read-only query language used to explore, analyze, and visualize data in Azure Monitor Log Analytics. It's optimized for large datasets and time-series analysis.

Intuitive Syntax

Designed for readability, KQL uses a pipe-delimited syntax (|) to chain operations.

Rich Functionality

Supports advanced filtering, aggregation, time-series functions, and machine learning capabilities.

Actionable Insights

Transforms raw log data into meaningful information for troubleshooting, security, and performance optimization.

Common KQL Operators

where: Filtering

Filters a table to the subset of rows that satisfy a predicate.

project: Selecting Columns

Selects the columns to include, rename, or drop, and inserts new computed columns.

summarize: Aggregation

Aggregates groups of rows into a single row by using functions like count(), avg(), sum().

extend & join: Advanced Operations

extend creates new calculated columns; join merges rows of two tables based on matching column values.

Key Takeaway

KQL is the essential language for querying Log Analytics, enabling sophisticated analysis of application logs to extract meaningful insights and troubleshoot effectively.

screens.title: Querying Function App Logs for Errors
screens.narratorSegment: Let's put KQL into practice with a common scenario: identifying errors within your Azure Function App logs. When a serverless function experiences intermittent failures, quickly finding the specific error messages and stack traces is paramount for debugging. The query you see on screen is designed to do just that. We start by specifying the Function App Logs table, which contains all the comprehensive logs for your Azure Functions. Next, we use the where operator to filter these logs. We're looking for entries where the Log Level is equal to 'Error'. This narrows down the vast amount of log data to only the critical issues. Then, the project operator is used to select only the columns that are most relevant for our investigation: Time Generated to see when the error occurred, Host Instance Id to identify the specific instance that processed the function, Function Name to know which function failed, and Message to get the actual error details. Finally, order by Time Generated desc sorts the results, showing the most recent errors first. This KQL query provides a targeted and efficient way to pinpoint and analyze errors, significantly reducing the time it takes to diagnose and resolve issues in your serverless applications. It's a fundamental query for any developer working with Azure Functions.

keyIdea.title: Targeted Error Identification
keyIdea.text: KQL allows precise filtering of Function App Logs to quickly identify error messages, providing crucial details like `TimeGenerated`, `HostInstanceId`, `FunctionName`, and `Message` for rapid debugging.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Querying Function App Logs for Errors

KQL Query: Function App Errors

FunctionAppLogs
| where LogLevel == "Error"
| project TimeGenerated, HostInstanceId, FunctionName, Message
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Query Explanation

FunctionAppLogs: Data Source

Specifies the table containing logs from your Azure Function Apps.

where LogLevel == "Error": Filtering

Filters the logs to include only entries where the severity level is 'Error'.

project TimeGenerated, ...: Column Selection

Selects specific columns (timestamp, host, function name, message) for focused analysis.

order by TimeGenerated desc: Sorting

Sorts the results in descending order by the time the log was generated, showing the most recent errors first.

Key Takeaway

This KQL query efficiently isolates and presents critical error information from Function App logs, enabling rapid diagnosis and troubleshooting of serverless application issues.

screens.title: Analyzing App Service HTTP Request Patterns

keyIdea.text: Using KQL, you can summarize HTTP request data for App Services to understand traffic patterns, identify popular endpoints, and detect performance bottlenecks based on request count and average latency.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Analyzing App Service HTTP Request Patterns

KQL Query: App Service HTTP Patterns

AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1h)
| summarize RequestCount = count(), AverageLatencyMs = avg(TimeTaken) by CsUriStem, HttpStatus
| order by RequestCount desc

Query Explanation

AppServiceHTTPLogs: Data Source

Specifies the table containing HTTP access logs for your Azure App Service.

where TimeGenerated > ago(1h): Time Filter

Filters logs to include only those generated within the last one hour.

summarize RequestCount = count(), ...: Aggregation

Calculates the total request count and average latency for each unique URI stem and HTTP status.

by CsUriStem, HttpStatus: Grouping

Groups the aggregated results by the requested URI path and the HTTP response status code.

Key Takeaway

This KQL query provides a powerful way to analyze App Service HTTP traffic, revealing request patterns, endpoint performance, and overall web application health at a glance.

screens.title: Setting Up Intelligent Alerts in Azure Monitor
screens.narratorSegment: While collecting and analyzing data is crucial, the cornerstone of proactive monitoring is intelligent alerting. Azure Monitor allows you to create alert rules that automatically notify you when specific conditions are met, transforming reactive firefighting into proactive incident management. There are two primary types of alerts we'll focus on: metric alerts and log alerts. Metric alerts are triggered when a specific metric's value crosses a predefined threshold. For example, you could set an alert if your App Service's C P U usage exceeds 80% for five consecutive minutes. Log alerts, on the other hand, are more flexible and powerful. They are triggered when a KQL query returns results that meet a specific condition, such as detecting more than ten 'Error' logs from your Function App within a five-minute window. When an alert fires, it can trigger various actions through what are called 'action groups'. These action groups define how you want to be notified, whether it's sending an email, an SMS, pushing a message to an ITSM tool like ServiceNow, or even triggering an Azure Function to automatically remediate an issue. The key is to configure these alerts and action groups thoughtfully to ensure the right people or systems are notified at the right time, preventing 'alert fatigue' and ensuring critical issues receive immediate attention. This proactive approach is vital for maintaining application reliability and minimizing downtime.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Setting Up Intelligent Alerts in Azure Monitor

Types of Azure Monitor Alerts

Metric Alerts

Triggered when a metric's value (e.g., CPU usage, HTTP response time) crosses a predefined threshold.

  • Threshold-based: Simple to configure for common performance indicators.
  • Real-time: Often evaluate conditions frequently for quick detection.
  • Example: CPU usage > 80% for 5 minutes.

Log Alerts

Triggered when a KQL query returns results that meet a specific condition (e.g., number of errors). More flexible.

  • Query-based: Leverage KQL for complex conditions and pattern matching.
  • Granular Control: Detect specific events or trends in your log data.
  • Example: >10 'Error' logs in the last 5 minutes.

Action Groups: The Response Mechanism

Collections of notification preferences and actions (e.g., email, SMS, webhook) triggered when an alert fires.

  • Notification Channels: Email, SMS, Push notifications, Voice call.
  • Automation: Webhooks, Azure Functions, ITSM tools for auto-remediation.
  • Customizable: Tailor responses to different alert severities and teams.
Key Takeaway

Azure Monitor alerts, both metric and log-based, combined with Action Groups, provide a robust framework for proactive incident detection and automated response, crucial for application reliability.

screens.title: Creating Metric Alerts with Azure CLI
screens.narratorSegment: Just as with diagnostic settings, creating metric alerts can also be automated using the Azure CLI, ensuring consistency and scalability across your monitoring setup. Let's examine how to create a metric alert for an App Service's C P U utilization. This example demonstrates how to set up an alert that triggers if the average C P U percentage exceeds 80% for a continuous period. The command az monitor metrics alert create is our starting point. We provide a descriptive name for the alert, specify its resource-group, and crucially, define the scopes which is the resource ID of our App Service. The condition parameter is where we define the logic: avg Percentage C P U greater than 80 means the alert will fire if the average C P U percentage metric goes above 80. We also add a description for clarity. evaluation-frequency 1m tells Azure Monitor to check the condition every minute, and window-size 5m means it will evaluate the average over the last five minutes. The severity level helps categorize the alert's urgency, and finally, we link it to an action group, which dictates how notifications are sent. A common mistake here is setting overly aggressive thresholds, leading to 'alert fatigue' where too many non-critical alerts desensitize your team. It's best to start with reasonable thresholds and refine them over time based on your application's baseline performance. This automated approach ensures your critical performance indicators are always under watchful eyes.

keyIdea.text: Automating metric alert creation via Azure CLI ensures consistent monitoring for critical performance indicators like CPU usage, allowing for proactive issue detection and notification while avoiding alert fatigue.

content.html:
Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Creating Metric Alerts with Azure CLI

Azure CLI for App Service CPU Alert

# Example: Create a metric alert for App Service CPU usage
# Replace <app-service-id> with your actual App Service resource ID
# Replace <action-group-id> with an existing action group ID (e.g., for email notifications)

az monitor metrics alert create \
    --name "HighCpuAlert" \
    --resource-group "MonitorDemoRG" \
    --scopes $APP_SERVICE_ID \
    --condition "avg PercentageCpu > 80" \
    --description "CPU usage for App Service is consistently high." \
    --evaluation-frequency 1m \
    --window-size 5m \
    --severity 2 \
    --action <action-group-id>

Command Breakdown & Best Practices

--scopes & --condition

Define the target resource (App Service ID) and the metric condition (e.g., average CPU > 80%).

--evaluation-frequency & --window-size

Set how often the condition is checked and over what period the metric is averaged.

--severity & --action

Assign an urgency level and link to an Action Group for notification methods.

Common Mistake: Alert Fatigue

Avoid overly aggressive thresholds. Start with reasonable values and refine them based on your application's baseline performance to prevent excessive, non-critical alerts.

Key Takeaway

Automating metric alert creation via Azure CLI ensures consistent monitoring for critical performance indicators, but careful threshold tuning is essential to avoid alert fatigue.

You can pin various components directly to a dashboard, creating a tailored view for different roles within your team, whether they are developers, operations staff, or even business owners. By consolidating all relevant monitoring data into a single, intuitive interface, dashboards empower your team to make informed decisions quickly, ensuring your applications remain reliable and performant. Module 6›Chapter 6.2›Visualizing Application Health with Azure Monitor Dashboards

Designing Effective Azure Monitor Dashboards

Customizable Visualization Layer

Consolidate metrics, logs, and Application Insights data into a single, intuitive view.

  • Pin Charts: Add metric explorer charts for performance trends.
  • Log Query Results: Visualize KQL query outputs (e.g., error counts over time).
  • App Insights Components: Integrate specific telemetry from Application Insights.

Highlight Critical KPIs

Focus on key performance indicators (KPIs) for rapid identification of potential problems.

  • Request Rates: Monitor incoming traffic volume.
  • Error Rates: Track the percentage of failed requests.
  • Latency: Observe application response times.
  • Resource Utilization: Keep an eye on CPU, memory, and network usage.

Tailored for Different Roles

Create multiple dashboards customized for the specific needs and focus areas of various team members.

  • Developer Dashboard: Focus on application logs, errors, and dependency performance.
  • Operations Dashboard: Emphasize infrastructure health, resource utilization, and alerts.
  • Business Owner Dashboard: Highlight user experience metrics, key transaction success rates.
Key Takeaway

Azure Monitor Dashboards are essential for providing a consolidated, real-time view of application health, enabling rapid problem identification and informed decision-making across your team.

They are triggered when a KQL query returns results that meet a specific condition, such as detecting more than ten 'Error' logs from your Function App within a five-minute window. When an alert fires, it can trigger various actions through what are called 'action groups'. These action groups define how you want to be notified, whether it's sending an email, an SMS, pushing a message to an ITSM tool like ServiceNow, or even triggering an Azure Function to automatically remediate an issue. The key is to configure these alerts and action groups thoughtfully to ensure the right people or systems are notified at the right time, preventing 'alert fatigue' and ensuring critical issues receive immediate attention. This proactive approach is vital for maintaining application reliability and minimizing downtime.

Just as with diagnostic settings, creating metric alerts can also be automated using the Azure CLI, ensuring consistency and scalability across your monitoring setup. Let's examine how to create a metric alert for an App Service's C P U utilization. This example demonstrates how to set up an alert that triggers if the average C P U percentage exceeds 80% for a continuous period. The command az monitor metrics alert create is our starting point. We provide a descriptive name for the alert, specify its resource-group, and crucially, define the scopes which is the resource ID of our App Service. The condition parameter is where we define the logic: avg Percentage C P U greater than 80 means the alert will fire if the average C P U percentage metric goes above 80. We also add a description for clarity. evaluation-frequency 1m tells Azure Monitor to check the condition every minute, and window-size 5m means it will evaluate the average over the last five minutes. The severity level helps categorize the alert's urgency, and finally, we link it to an action group, which dictates how notifications are sent. A common mistake here is setting overly aggressive thresholds, leading to 'alert fatigue' where too many non-critical alerts desensitize your team. It's best to start with reasonable thresholds and refine them over time based on your application's baseline performance. This automated approach ensures your critical performance indicators are always under watchful eyes.

Finally, to bring all your monitoring data together into a cohesive and easily digestible format, Azure Monitor Dashboards provide a customizable visualization layer. Think of a dashboard as your application's command center, offering a quick, real-time overview of its health and performance at a glance. You can pin various components directly to a dashboard, creating a tailored view for different roles within your team, whether they are developers, operations staff, or even business owners. For instance, you can pin charts from the metric explorer to visualize C P U usage or request rates, display results from your KQL log queries to show error trends, and even integrate specific components from Application Insights for deep telemetry. A well-designed dashboard is crucial because it highlights critical Key Performance Indicators, or KPIs, such as request rates, error rates, latency, and resource utilization. This enables rapid identification of potential problems without having to navigate through multiple Azure services. By consolidating all relevant monitoring data into a single, intuitive interface, dashboards empower your team to make informed decisions quickly, ensuring your applications remain reliable and performant. Remember to regularly review and adjust your dashboards as your application evolves to keep them relevant and effective.

Let's recap some of the essential concepts we've covered in this chapter, starting with the different types of application logging. First, 'Application Logging' refers to capturing logs generated directly by your application code, such as messages from Console. Write Line. These are crucial for debugging your specific business logic and understanding what your code is doing. Next, 'Web Server Logging' focuses on recording HTTP request details for web applications. This includes information like request methods, URLs, status codes, and latency, providing insights into traffic patterns and web server performance. Finally, 'Function App Logs' are the comprehensive logs specifically for Azure Functions. These logs encompass host logs, controller logs, and function-specific events, giving you a complete picture of your serverless function's execution and any issues it might encounter. Understanding these distinct logging categories is fundamental to configuring effective diagnostic settings and ensuring you collect the right data for your monitoring needs.

Continuing our review of key concepts, let's focus on how we proactively detect and visualize issues. 'Metric Alerts' are automated notifications triggered when a metric's value, such as C P U usage or HTTP latency, crosses a predefined threshold. These are straightforward for common performance indicators. Complementing these are 'Log Alerts', which are automated notifications triggered when a Kusto Query Language, or KQL, query returns results that meet a specific condition. This allows for more complex and granular detection based on patterns in your log data. When an alert fires, it utilizes 'Action Groups', which are collections of notification preferences and actions. These define how you're notified—be it email, SMS, or even triggering an automated remediation via a webhook or Azure Function. Finally, 'Azure Monitor Dashboards' provide a customizable visual display that consolidates metrics, logs, and other monitoring data. They offer a quick, real-time overview of your application's health and performance, enabling rapid identification of potential problems. Together, these concepts form a robust framework for proactive monitoring, ensuring your applications remain reliable and performant.
